Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verses 1–2:

(p-39) (Sūrat al-Zukhruf is Meccan, though it is said that the exception is His saying "And ask those whom We sent before you," and its verses number eighty-nine.)

﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ The discussion concerning it is like that which has passed concerning the opening of Sūrat Yā Sīn, except that the apparent meaning, on the assumption that it is a noun, is that it is a name for the Qur'an and not for the surah, as has been said, for that would impair the eloquence of the noble composition.

﴿Wa-l-Kitābi l-Mubīn﴾

﴿Wa-l-Kitābi⦆ in the genitive (bi-l-jarr), on the basis that it is an oath sworn by it, either as a new beginning or as a conjunction with "Ḥā Mīm," on the assumption that it is in the genitive by the implied particle of oath (bā' al-qasam), on the basis that the basis of the conjunction is the difference in the heading, and the reason for honouring the oath is the emphasis on confirming the content of the oath-sentence.

﴿Al-Mubīn⦆ meaning: the clear one, for those to whom it was revealed, because it is in their tongue and in their styles; or the one that makes clear the path of guidance from the path of misguidance, the one that elucidates everything that is needed in matters of religion.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verses 1–2:

(p-39) (Sūrat al-Zukhruf is Meccan, though it is said that the exception is His saying "And ask those whom We sent before you," and its verses number eighty-nine.)

﴿Ḥā Mīm﴾ The discussion concerning it is like that which has passed concerning the opening of Sūrat Yā Sīn, except that the apparent meaning, on the assumption that it is a noun, is that it is a name for the Qur'an and not for the surah, as has been said, for that would impair the eloquence of the noble composition.

﴿Wa-l-Kitābi l-Mubīn﴾

﴿Wa-l-Kitābi⦆ in the genitive (bi-l-jarr), on the basis that it is an oath sworn by it, either as a new beginning or as a conjunction with "Ḥā Mīm," on the assumption that it is in the genitive by the implied particle of oath (bā' al-qasam), on the basis that the basis of the conjunction is the difference in the heading, and the reason for honouring the oath is the emphasis on confirming the content of the oath-sentence.

﴿Al-Mubīn⦆ meaning: the clear one, for those to whom it was revealed, because it is in their tongue and in their styles; or the one that makes clear the path of guidance from the path of misguidance, the one that elucidates everything that is needed in matters of religion.

Indeed, ﴿We have made it an Arabic Qur'an﴾ is the response to the oath (jawab al-qasam), but not in the sense that the emphasis attaches to the act of making it so, as has been said. Rather, the emphasis attaches to its purpose, which is expressed by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so that you may understand﴾. For that purpose is what needs confirmation and emphasis, since it indicates care for their affairs, the completion of His blessing upon them, and the removal of their excuses. That is: We made that Book an Arabic Qur'an so that you may understand it and comprehend the excellent arrangement and the surpassing meaning within it, and become aware of the clear proofs it contains that show it is beyond the capacity of humankind, and recognize the true worth of the blessing in that, and that your excuses be cut off entirely.

﴿And indeed it is in the Mother of the Book﴾, meaning in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz), for it is the origin of the heavenly books. It is also read as "إمِّ الكِتابِ" (Immi al-Kitab) with a kasra.

﴿with Us﴾, meaning with Us.

﴿is exalted﴾, meaning of high rank and noble among the books.

﴿full of wisdom﴾, meaning possessing far-reaching wisdom, or "firmly established" (muhkam). These two are predicates of inna, and what lies between them is an explanation of the place of the judgment, as if it were said: after explaining its attribute of the two sublime qualities mentioned, "it is in the Mother of the Book" and "with Us." The sentence is either a conjunction with the sentence that the oath is sworn upon, and falls under its ruling. In that case, swearing by the Qur'an to establish its high rank with Him, the Exalted, displays a wondrous eloquence and signals that its loftiness is such that explaining it does not require citing an oath by anything else. Rather, it is by itself sufficient as a testimony to that, in that it is sworn by, just as it is sufficient as testimony in terms of its inimitability. It also indicates that, when it is mentioned, nothing else comes to mind as more fitting to be sworn by. Or it is a resumptive (mustanafah) sentence confirming its loftiness, which the oath pointed to, in the manner of an interjection (i'tiraD) in His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And indeed it is a great oath, if you only knew﴾ (p-40). After clarifying the loftiness of the great Qur'an, and establishing that its revelation in their language was so that they would understand it, believe in it, and act according to its requirements, he follows this with a denial that the matter could be otherwise, and so it is said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 5:

﴿Shall We then turn away the Reminder from you﴾ i.e., We remove it and keep it away from you. It is a metaphor (majaz) drawn from the saying of them, "driving the strangers away from the basin" (ḍarb al-gharā'ib 'an al-ḥawḍ). It also carries an indication that wisdom requires the Reminder to be directed toward them and to remain attached to them, as though it were falling upon them. The fa' (then) is a conjunction (li-l-'atf) upon an elided element that the context requires, i.e., "Shall We then leave you alone and remove the Reminder from you?"

﴿Ṣafḥan﴾ i.e., turning away from you. It may be a object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu) for the verb mentioned, or an emphatic infinitive (maṣdar mu'akkid) for what the verb itself indicates, since removing (al-tanḥiyah) definitely signifies turning away and aversion (al-ṣafḥ wa-al-i'rāḍ). It is as if it were said: "Shall We surely turn away from you with aversion?" Or it may carry the meaning of "side" (al-jānib), in which case it is in the accusative of place (al-ẓarfiyyah), i.e., "Shall We remove it from you to one side?"

﴿Because you have been a people who exceed the bounds﴾ i.e., because you have been immersed in extravagance and persist in it, in the sense that your state, although it would require that We leave you to yourselves until you die in disbelief and error and remain in the everlasting punishment, nevertheless, out of the vastness of Our mercy, We do not do that; rather We guide you to the truth by sending the trustworthy Messenger and sending down the clear Book. It has also been read as "in" (in) with a kasra, on the basis that the clause is conditional, presenting what is certain as though it were doubtful, due to their ignorance (istijhālihim). The apodosis (jazā') is elided, relying on what precedes it as an indication.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verses 6–7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples?﴾ and ﴿And there never came to them a prophet but that they used to mock him.﴾ is a confirmation (taqrir) of what precedes it, by explaining that the excess (israf) of the earlier nations did not prevent Him, exalted is He, from sending prophets to them; and it is a consolation (tasliyah) to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding the mockery of his people toward him.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verses 6–7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And how many a prophet did We send among the earlier peoples?﴾ and ﴿And there never came to them a prophet but that they used to mock him.﴾ is a confirmation (taqrir) of what precedes it, by explaining that the excess (israf) of the earlier nations did not prevent Him, exalted is He, from sending prophets to them; and it is a consolation (tasliyah) to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) regarding the mockery of his people toward him.

Abu al-Su'ud's commentary (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 8:

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So We destroyed those who were stronger than them in might﴾, meaning: from among these profligate people, [He is giving] a promise to the Messenger (ﷺ) and a threat to them of the same fate that befell the earlier peoples. Describing them as stronger in might is to establish the ruling against these people by way of a fortiori (al-awlawiyyah).

﴿And the example of the earlier peoples has already passed﴾, meaning: the account of them, which is worthy of becoming a proverb, has already been mentioned in the Qur'an more than once.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 9:

﴿And if you were to ask them, "Who created the heavens and the earth?" they would surely say, "They were created by the Almighty, the All-Knowing."﴾ That is: they would surely attribute their creation to the One whose state in reality and in fact is such, not that they would express Him by this title. The adoption of this manner is to indicate that His being characterized by what has been enumerated of sublime attributes and acts, and by what this entails of resurrection and recompense, is a matter that is clear and beyond doubt, and that the proof stands against them, whether they wish or refuse. It has also been permitted that this itself be the very wording they use.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 10:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Who has made the earth for you a cradle﴾ is a resumptive statement from Him, may He be exalted, meaning: He spread it out for you, so that you may settle upon it.

﴿And has made for you therein roads﴾ that you may travel along in your journeys.

﴿That you may perhaps be guided﴾, meaning: so that you may be guided by traveling them to your destinations, or by reflecting upon them toward Tawhid (the Oneness of God), which is the primary aim.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 11:

﴿And He who sends down water from the sky in measure﴾ in a measure required by His will, which is founded upon wisdoms and benefits.

﴿So We revive thereby﴾ i.e., We bring to life by that water.

﴿a dead land﴾ empty of growth and vegetation altogether. It is also read "maytan" (mayyitan) with doubled ya', and its masculine form (mayt) is because al-baldah is in the sense of al-balad (the land/place). The shift to the first-person plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah) serves to show complete care for the matter of giving life and to indicate its great importance.

﴿Thus﴾ i.e., like that revival, which in reality is the bringing forth of plants from the earth.

﴿you will be brought forth﴾ i.e., you will be raised from your graves alive. In expressing the bringing forth of plants by "inshar," which is the reviving of the dead, and expressing their revival by "ikhraj," there is an exaltation of the matter of plant growth and a making light of the matter of resurrection, in order to straighten the paths of inference and clarify the method of analogy.

﴿Who created all the pairs﴾, i.e., the kinds of created things. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that "the pairs" are the types and varieties, such as the sweet and the sour, the white and the black, and the male and the female. It was also said: everything other than Allah the Exalted is a pair, such as above and below, right and left, and so on.

﴿And He made for you of the ships and the cattle that which you ride﴾, i.e., that which you ride, giving precedence to the cattle over the ships (taghlib, a rhetorical device of giving one of two mentioned items precedence over the other). The verb for riding is transitive by itself, and its use with ships and the like with the preposition "fi" (in) alludes to their being a container and to the fact that their movement is not by one's own will, as has passed in Surat Hud at His saying: ﴿And he said, "Embark therein"﴾.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 13:

﴿That you may sit firmly upon their backs﴾ i.e., that you may be elevated upon the backs of what you ride of the ships and the cattle. The plural is used in view of the meaning.

﴿Then you may remember the favour of your Lord when you are settled upon them﴾ i.e., that you remember it in your hearts, acknowledging it and esteeming it greatly, and then praise Him for it with your tongues.

﴿And say: Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us﴾, expressing wonder at that, as is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that when he put his foot in the stirrup he would say, "In the name of Allah," and when he was settled upon the mount he would say, "Praise be to Allah for every condition. Glory be to Him who has subjected this to us," up to His saying, Most High: ﴿And to our Lord indeed we are returning﴾, and he would say "Allahu akbar" three times and "La ilaha illa Allah" three times.

﴿And we were not capable of it﴾ i.e., we were not able to master it. It is from aqran al-shay' (to make something submit), when one is able to subdue it; its root meaning is finding a companion (qarinah) for it, because a difficult thing cannot be a companion to a weak one. It is also read with the shaddah (muqarrinin), and the meaning is one. This is part of the completion of the mention of His favour, Most High, for without the one who receives the favour acknowledging his inability to obtain the favour, its worth is not known, nor is the right of the Benefactor in it.

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿And indeed, to our Lord we are surely returning.﴾ Meaning: returning (ارجعون).

Translation of the commentary:

"Meaning: returning." In this there is an indication that it is incumbent upon the rider to reflect on the journey he is engaged in, and to remember through it the greater journey, which is the return (inqilab) to God Most High. Thus he should build his affairs during that journey upon this awareness, and it should never occur to his mind anything of what he does, nor should he abandon any matter that contradicts it. And it is necessary for him that his riding be for a lawful purpose.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 15:

﴿And they have attributed to Him from among His servants a part.﴾ This is connected to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you asked them﴾ ... etc. That is: they have ascribed to Him, glorified is He, with their tongues and their beliefs, after that acknowledgment, a son from among His servants. He expressed it as a "part" (juz') only to emphasize its impossibility with respect to the One True God in every respect. It has also been read as "juzu'" (juzʾ) with two dammas.

﴿Indeed, the human being is an evident ungrateful disbeliever.﴾ Manifest ingratitude (kufran), exaggerated in degree; and for this reason they say what they say. Glory be to Allah above what they describe.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 16:

﴿Has He taken for Himself daughters out of what He creates?﴾ "Am" (أمْ) is *munqati'a* (disjunctive, i.e. introducing a new question), and what it carries of meaning is "bal" (بَلْ, "rather"), for the transition from explaining the falsity of their attributing to Him, exalted is He, a child absolutely, to explaining the falsity of their attributing that child to the lowest of its two kinds. The *hamza* (الهمزة, the interrogative particle) is for denunciation, rebuke and wonder at their state. His statement, exalted is He, ﴿and has He preferred you with sons?﴾ is either a conjunction (*'atf*) upon "ittakhadha" (اتَّخَذَ, "has taken"), falling under the ruling of denunciation and wonder, which is the well-known difference of opinion, and the turning to their address (*iltifat*, a shift from third-person to second-person speech) is for emphasizing the obligation and intensifying the rebuke. That is: "Rather, has He taken from His creation the lowest?" Or it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from its doer, with "qad" (قَدْ) implied or not, "upon the two kinds," and He chose for you the better of them. The meaning is: Suppose you have been bold enough to attribute the taking of the kind of child to Him, glory be to Him, despite the evident impossibility and impermissibility of it, did you not have any portion of intellect or any trace of shame, so that you became bold enough to utter the monstrous claim that shatters minds: that He, exalted is He, preferred you over Himself with the better and higher of the two kinds, and left Himself the worse and lower of them? The indefinite "banat" (بَناتٍ, "daughters") and the definite "al-banin" (البَنِينَ, "the sons") are for displaying what is considered in each of them of lowliness and grandeur.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 17:

﴿And when one of them is given good news of that which he attributes to the Most Merciful as a likeness...﴾ ...etc. This is a resumptive clause (isti'naf muqarrir) confirming what precedes it. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: they ascribed to Him what they mentioned, and among their states is that when one of them is given good news of it, he is distressed. The shift in address (iltifat) is to signal that mentioning their ugly conduct calls for turning away from them and relating it to others, in wonder at it; that is: when one of them is informed of the birth of that which he made a likeness for Him, Glorified is He, since a child must be of the same kind as its parent and resemble it.

﴿His face becomes darkened﴾, meaning: it becomes utterly black from the evil of what he was given good news of.

﴿And he is inwardly filled with grief (kazim)﴾, meaning: filled with anguish and sorrow. The clause is circumstantial (hal). It has been read as "musawwad" and "musawadd," with the pronoun of the one given the good news in "zalla" and "wajhuhu musawwad" forming a clause that serves as its predicate.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 18:

﴿Or is one who is brought up in ornaments﴾ is a repetition of the denunciation and a second rebuke. "Man" (مَن) is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb conjoined to "ja'alū" (they ascribed), meaning: "Or have they ascribed to Allah one who is brought up in ornament, and who is incapable of managing his own affairs?" So the hamza (الهَمْزَةُ, the interrogative particle) is for denouncing the actual act and deeming it abhorrent. It has also been permitted that its accusative governs an implied verb conjoined to "ittakhadha" (took), so the hamza then serves to deny the occurrence and to deem it unlikely. Its placement between the two conjoined elements serves to recall the denunciation contained in "am" (أم) when it is disjunctive (مُنْقَطِعَةً), and to emphasise it. The conjunction serves to indicate a difference in description (لِلتَّغايُرِ العُنْوانِيِّ): "Or has He taken for Himself, from among this blameworthy attribute, that attribute of his?"

﴿And he﴾ together with what has been mentioned of deficiency.

﴿in disputation﴾ meaning: in contention, which a human being customarily scarcely ever is free from.

﴿is not clear [in expression]﴾ meaning: not able to establish his claim and present his proof, due to the deficiency of his intellect and the weakness of his judgement. The addition of "ghayr" (غَيْرُ) does not prevent what follows it from governing the preceding prepositional phrase, because it carries the sense of negation. It has also been read (p-43) "yunsha'u" (يُنْشَأُ) and "yunasha'u" (يُناشَأُ), from the forms of "af'ala" (الإفْعالِ) and "mufa'ala" (المُفاعَلَةِ); all carry one meaning, and their parallel is "ghallāhu", "aghlāhu" and "ghālāhu" (meaning: he made it expensive).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 19:

﴿And they have made the angels, who are the servants of the Most Merciful, females.﴾ This is an explanation that their aforementioned disbelief implies another disbelief, and a rebuke to them for it, namely their making the most noble of servants and the most honored of them before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, the most deficient in judgment and the basest of kinds. It has been read as "ʿabīd al-Raḥmān" (servants/slaves of the Most Merciful), and as "ʿinda al-Raḥmān" (with the Most Merciful), depicting their closeness (zulfā) to Him. It has also been read as "unithan" (ʾunuth), which is a plural of a plural (jamʿ al-jamʿ).

﴿Did they witness their creation?﴾ That is: did they attend the creation of Allah, Exalted is He, of them, so that they witnessed them as females and thereby judged them to be female? For that is something known by direct observation. This is a declaration of their ignorance and a mockery of them. It has been read as "a-ushhidū" with two hamzas, the first open and the second dammed, and as "ā-ushhidū" with an alif between them.

﴿Their testimony will be recorded﴾: this, in the register of their deeds.

﴿And they will be questioned﴾ about it on the Day of Resurrection. It has been read as "sayaktubu" and "sanaktubu" with the yāʾ and the nūn respectively. It has also been read as "shahādātuhum" (their testimonies), namely their saying that Allah has a part (juzʾ) and that He has daughters, and that they are the angels. It has been read as "yasʾalūna" from al-masʾalah (questioning), for emphasis (lil-mubālaghah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 20:

﴿And they say: "If the Most Merciful had willed, we would not have worshipped them."﴾ This is an explanation of another kind of their disbelief, meaning: if the Most Merciful had willed our not worshipping the angels with the will of approval (mashiyyat irtida'), we would not have worshipped them. By this they intended to show that what they did is true and approved by Him, Exalted is He, and that they only do it by His Exalted will for them, while acknowledging its ugliness, so that their blame by it would stand as proof for the Mu'tazilah. The foundation of their false statement rests on two premises: the first is that their worship of them is by His Exalted will, and the second is that this necessarily implies it is approved by Him, Exalted is He. They erred in the second premise, for they were ignorant that will (mashi'ah) is an expression for preferring some possibilities over others, whatever they may be, without considering approval or disapproval in either of the two sides. For this reason they were ignorant of His Exalted saying: ﴿They have no knowledge of that﴾, meaning: of what they intended by their saying that what they did was by the will of approval and not by mere will. For this is established, and countless noble verses speak to it.

﴿Of knowledge﴾, that is, resting on any authority.

﴿They merely guess﴾, that is, they fabricate baselessly. It has also been permitted that by this he refers to the root of the claim, as if, having displayed the aspects of its corruption and related their discredited doubts, he denied that they have knowledge of it by way of reason, then turned away from that to refute that they have any authority from the side of transmission. Then it is said:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 21:

﴿Or have We given them a Book before this [Qur'an], so that they hold fast to it?﴾ "Before it" means before the Qur'an, or before their claim, a Book that testifies to the soundness of what they claim.

﴿So they hold fast by it﴾ by that Book.

﴿Holding firmly﴾ and relying upon it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 22:

﴿Nay, but they say: "We found our fathers following a religion, and we are guided in their footsteps."﴾ That is: they did not bring any rational or traditional proof; rather, they acknowledged that they have no basis except the blind imitation (taqlid) of their fathers, who were ignorant like them. And "al-ummah" (community, religion) is the path (din and tariqah) that is aimed at (tu'amm), i.e., intended, like the journey (al-rihlah) toward that to which one travels. It has also been read as "immah" with a kasra, which is the state in which the one who aims (al-amm), i.e., the one who intends, is. As for His exalted saying, ﴿upon their footsteps are guided﴾, the two are predicates (khabarani), and the adverbial phrase (al-zarf) is a complement (silah) to "muhtadun" (guided).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 23:

﴿And thus﴾ i.e., the matter is as mentioned: their inability to produce proof and their clinging to the hem of blind imitation (taqlid). His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿We never sent before you a warner into any town but its affluent ones said, "Indeed we found our fathers upon a religion, and indeed we are following in their footsteps."﴾ is a resumed statement (isti'naf) explaining that, denoting that imitation among them is an ancient error, for their forefathers too had no basis for it other than this. The singling out of the affluent (mutrafun) for that statement is to signal (li'l-idhan) that luxury and love of idleness are what diverted them from reflective inquiry toward imitation.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 24:**

﴿He said﴾: a narration of what took place between the warners and their peoples when the peoples made excuses by imitating their forefathers. That is, each warner among those warners said to his people:

﴿Even if I came to you﴾: that is, "Will you follow your forefathers even if I came to you

﴿with a religion more guided﴾: with a more guided religion

﴿than that upon which you found your forefathers﴾: than the misguidance upon which you found your forefathers, which has nothing of guidance in it. He expressed it in this way only by accommodating them, following the path of fairness. It has also been read as "Say" (qul), as the narration of a past command that was revealed at that time to every warner, not as an address to the Messenger ﷺ, as has been said, because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They said: Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you have been sent﴾. This is definitely a narration about the peoples, meaning: each community said to its warner, "Indeed we disbelieve in that with which you were sent..." etc. The speech was summarized in the narration for brevity, as was explained before in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾. Taking it as a narration about his own people, peace be upon him, by reading the plural form as a figure of speech of prevalence (taghlib) that gives him precedence over the rest of the warners, peace be upon them, and by directing their disbelief to what all of them were sent with, which is monotheism, because they all agreed on it, as in the parallels to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿'Ad denied the messengers﴾, is a far-fetched contrivance, which is entirely refuted by His saying, exalted is He:

﴿So We took vengeance upon them﴾, that is, by annihilation.

﴿Then look at how was the end of those who denied﴾ among the nations mentioned, so do not be concerned about the denial of your people.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 26:

﴿And when Abraham said﴾ — that is: recall for them the time when he, peace be upon him, said ﴿to his father and his people﴾ — those who were devoted to imitation (taqlid) — how he disavowed what they were engaged in, by saying: ﴿Indeed, I am free from what you worship﴾, and he held fast to the proof, so that they might follow his method of reasoning (istidlal), or, if they had no alternative to imitation, so that they might imitate him, for he was the most noble of their forefathers. "Bara'" (barā᾽) is a verbal noun (maṣdar) used as an adjective for emphasis (mubalaghah); for this reason it is used in the same form for the singular and plural, and for the masculine and feminine. It has also been read as "barī'" (بَرِيءٌ) and "buarā'" (بُراءٌ) with a dammah on the bā᾽, like karīm and kirām. The "mā" (ما) is either a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle or a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah) whose returning pronoun has been omitted, meaning: "Indeed, I am free from your worship or from what you worship."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 27:

﴿Except He who created me, for He will guide me.﴾

The phrase ﴿إلا الَّذِي فَطَرَنِي﴾ ("except He who created me") is an exceptive clause (istithna') which may be munqati' (disjunctive, i.e. "but") or muttasil (connected), on the basis that ما (ma) is general, encompassing those endowed with knowledge (ulu al-'ilm) and others, and that they used to worship Allah and the idols. Alternatively, it is a descriptive qualifier (sifah), on the basis that "ma" is qualified, meaning: "Indeed, I am free of the gods you worship, other than He who created me."

﴿فَإنَّهُ سَيَهْدِينِ﴾ ("for He will guide me") means: He will keep me firm upon guidance; or He will guide me to what lies beyond that to which He has guided me until now. The more correct view is that the sin (السين, sin) is for emphasis (lil-ta'kid) and not for deferment (lil-taswif), and the form of the present tense (صيغة المضارع, sigha al-mudari') indicates continuity (lil-dalalah 'ala al-istimrar).

**[Verse 43:28]** ﴿And He made it﴾: that is, Ibrahim made the word of monotheism, which he uttered, a reference to it.

﴿a word that endures among his descendants﴾: that is, among his offspring, since he enjoined it upon them, as expressed by the saying of the Exalted: ﴿And Ibrahim enjoined it upon his sons, and [so did] Ya'qub﴾ [2:132], and so there will always remain among them someone who affirms the oneness of God the Exalted and calls to His monotheism. It is also read as "kalimah" and "fi 'aqbihi" with the lightened pronunciation.

﴿that they may return﴾: this is a reason for the making. That is, He made it endure among his descendants in hope that whoever among them has associated partners [with God] would return to it through the call of the one who affirms the oneness [of God].

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 29:

﴿Nay, I gave enjoyment to these people﴾ — an idrab (a turning away, a shift from a previous topic, a term of grammar meaning a transition) from an omitted element that the discourse drives toward, as if it were said: He made it (the word) a lasting word among his descendants, by enjoining it upon his sons in the hope that those among them who associated partners would return to it through the supplication of the monotheist. But what he hoped for did not come about; rather, I gave enjoyment to these, the contemporaries of the Messenger ﷺ, from among the people of Makkah.

﴿and their fathers﴾ — with extension in life and blessing, so they were deceived by the respite and immersed themselves in desires and were occupied by them away from the word of tawhid (monotheism).

﴿until there came to them﴾ — that is, these people.

﴿the truth﴾ — that is, the Qur'an.

﴿and a manifest messenger﴾ — that is, a messenger.

﴿manifest﴾ — clear in the matter of his mission and evident in it through the dazzling miracles; or, making clear (tawhid) through the clear signs and proofs. It was also read as "matta'na" and "matta'ta" in the second person, on the basis that God Himself interjected it against His own essence in His saying: ﴿And He made it a lasting word﴾ ...etc. It is an intensification in describing their condition, for enjoyment through increased blessings obliges them to make it a cause for increased thankfulness and steadfastness upon tawhid and faith; but He made it a cause for increased ingratitude, the utmost degree of disbelief and misguidance.

And when the truth came to them, (the Qur'an) to awaken them from the heedlessness they were in and to guide them to tawhid (affirmation of God's oneness), they increased in disbelief, became insolent, and added to their earlier disbelief the obstinate opposition to the truth and the contempt for it, when ﴿they said, "This is sorcery, and we are disbelievers in it."﴾ So they named the Qur'an "sorcery," disbelieved in it, and held the Messenger (ﷺ) in contempt.

And they said, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two towns?"

"From the two towns": that is, from one of the two towns, Makkah and al-Ta'if, following the pattern of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from both of them come forth the pearl and the coral﴾.

"Of importance": that is, in rank and wealth, such as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi and Urwa ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. It is said: Habib ibn 'Amr ibn 'Umayr al-Thaqafi. And on the authority of Mujahid: 'Utba ibn Rabi'a and Kinana ibn 'Abd Yalil. They did not utter this great statement out of envy at its being sent down to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rather than to any of the great men of theirs who have been mentioned, along with their acknowledgment of its Qur'anic character. Rather, they were arguing for its non-Qur'anic status by way of the meaning: that if it were a Qur'an, it would have been sent down to one of these, according to what they claimed, namely that prophethood is a lofty office that befits none but one who has greatness in terms of wealth and rank. They did not realize that it is a spiritual rank, which none ascends to except the aspirations of the elect, who are singled out by pure souls, supported by holy power, and adorned with human virtues. As for those who are adorned with worldly ornaments and enjoy base worldly portions, they are a thousand stations away from deserving that rank.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 32:

(p-46) And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord? We have apportioned among them their livelihood in the life of this world, and raised some of them above others in degrees, so that some of them may take others in service (sukhriyyan). And the mercy of your Lord is better than what they accumulate.﴾

﴿Is it they who apportion the mercy of your Lord?﴾ This is a rebuke containing a declaration of their ignorance and an expression of wonder at their presumption. By "mercy" is meant prophethood.

﴿We have apportioned among them their livelihood﴾ i.e., the means of their livelihood.

﴿in the life of this world﴾ by a division required by Our will, which is founded on wisdom and benefit, and We did not entrust its affair to them, knowing their inability to manage it entirely.

﴿and raised some of them above others﴾ in provision and in the rest of the foundations of livelihood.

﴿in degrees﴾ varying according to nearness and remoteness, as wisdom requires: so there is the weak and the strong, the poor and the rich, the servant and the served, the ruler and the ruled.

﴿so that some of them may take others in service (sukhriyyan)﴾ so that some may direct others in their affairs, employ them in their professions, and make them work at their tasks, until they live together, assist one another, and reach their necessities, not for the perfection of the wealthy nor for the deficiency of the straitened. Had We left that to their management, they would have been lost and perished. If they are in this state regarding the management of their own petty affairs and what sustains them of the base goods of this world, which are but a trifle, then what do they think of themselves in managing the affair of religion, which is further removed than the Pleiades (al-'Ayyuq)? And from where would they have the capacity to search into the matter of prophethood and to choose for it one who is fit for it and will bear its charge?

﴿And the mercy of your Lord﴾ i.e., prophethood and what follows it of the happiness of both abodes.

﴿is better than what they accumulate﴾ of the perishable, base trash of this world.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And were it not that mankind would become one community, We would have given to those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses﴾ is a resumptive clause (*isti'naf*) that clarifies the insignificance of the goods of this world and the lowliness of their worth in the sight of God, Mighty and Majestic. The meaning is that the worthlessness of this world is such that, were it not that people, out of their love of this world, would not desire disbelief upon seeing its adherents in abundance and luxury, and thus gather around it, We would have given it in its entirety to the worst of creation and the lowest in rank. This is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We would have made for those who disbelieve in the Most Merciful silver roofs for their houses﴾, meaning made of silver. "*Li-buyutihim*" (لِبُيُوتِهِمْ) is a comprehensive apposition (*badal al-ishtimal*, a substitute that includes what it replaces) for "*li-man*" (لِمَن). The plural pronoun is used in accordance with the meaning of "*man*", just as the singular concealed pronoun in "*yakfuru*" (يَكْفُرُ) is used in accordance with its wording. "*Suqufan*" (سُقُفًا) is the plural of "*saqf*", like "*ruhun*" (رُهُنٌ) being the plural of "*rahn*". It is also reported from al-Farra' that it is the plural of "*saqifa*", like "*sufun*" (سُفُنٌ) being the plural of "*safina*". It was read as "*suqfan*" (سُقْفًا) with the qaf sukun for lightness, and as "*saqfan*" (سَقْفًا) by suffice with the plural "*buyut*" (houses). "*Suqufan*" (سُقُفًا) appears to be a dialectal form of "*saqf*" (سَقْفٍ), with the plural "*suqufan*" (سُقُوفًا).

﴿And stairways﴾, meaning We would have made for them stairways of silver, that is, ascents, the plural of "*ma'raj*" (مَعْرَجٍ). It was also read as "*ma'arij*" (مَعارِيجَ), the plural of "*mi'raj*" (مِعْراجٍ).

﴿upon which they would ascend﴾, meaning they would climb up onto the roofs and the high places.

ﷺ not needed here. Translating the passage:

﴿And for their houses﴾ That is: and We would make for their houses.

﴿Doors and couches﴾ of silver.

﴿Upon which﴾ That is: upon the couches.

﴿They would recline﴾ Perhaps the repetition of the mention of their houses is for the sake of emphasis and confirmation (taqrir).

**And ornaments of gold.** That is, adornment. It is coordinated with "roofs" (suqufan), or "gold" is coordinated with the grammatical position of "silver" (min fiddah).

**And all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the life of this world.** That is: all that has been mentioned of the houses, described with the detailed attributes, is only something enjoyed in the life of this world. Having the same meaning is what has been recited: "And all of that is nothing but the enjoyment of the life of this world." It has also been read with the "ma" lightened, taking "an" as the lightened form (mukhaffafah) and the lam as the distinguishing lam (al-lam al-fariqah). It has also been read with the lam kasrah, taking it as the lam of causation (lam al-'illah) and "ma" as a relative pronoun (mawsulah) whose returning pronoun has been omitted, meaning: "for that which is the enjoyment of ... etc.," as in His exalted words: ﴿Completion [of favor] upon the one who did good﴾.

**And the Hereafter** with its various kinds of blessings, which speech falls short of describing, **is with your Lord for the righteous** (al-muttaqin), that is, those who guard themselves against disbelief and sins. By this it becomes clear that the truly great is the great in the Hereafter, not in this world.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 36:

﴿And whoever turns blind⁠﴾ i.e., makes himself blind (yataʿammaa).

﴿to the remembrance of the Most Merciful⁠﴾ which is the Qur'an. Its attribution to the name al-Rahman is to signal (li-l-idhan) its descent as a mercy to the worlds. It has been read as "yaʿsha" with a fatḥah, meaning "yaʿma" (becomes blind). It is said: ʿasha yaʿshaa (ʿashā) when there is a defect in his sight, and ʿashaa yaʿshū when he makes himself blind without any defect, like ʿaraja and ʿaruja (both meaning "to limp"). It has also been read as "yaʿshū", on the basis that "man" is a relative pronoun (mawsūla) not implying the meaning of a conditional. The meaning is: whoever turns away from it, due to his excessive preoccupation with the splendour of the worldly life and his immersion in its perishable pleasures and desires.

﴿We appoint for him a devil, and he is his constant companion⁠﴾ who does not part from him and never ceases to whisper to him and lead him astray. It has been read as "yuqayyiḍ" with the yāʾ, attributing it to the pronoun of al-Rahman. And whoever reads "yaʿshū" with a ḍammah on the verb, then the correct reading for "yuqayyiḍ" is with a ḍammah too.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 37:

﴿And indeed they﴾ — i.e., the devils, each of whom has been assigned to each of those who are blind (to the remembrance of the Most Merciful).

﴿would surely bar them﴾ — i.e., their companions. The basis for the plurality of the two pronouns is the consideration of the meaning of "man" (man, "whoever"), just as the basis for the singularity of the preceding pronouns is the consideration of its wording.

﴿from the Way﴾ — the clear one, to which the Qur'an calls.

﴿and they think﴾ — i.e., those who are blind.

﴿that they﴾ — i.e., the devils.

﴿are rightly guided﴾ — i.e., to the straight Way; for otherwise they would not follow them. Or: they think that they themselves are rightly guided, because the belief that the devils are rightly guided entails the belief that they are likewise, since their course is one and the same. The clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the object of "yasuddunahum" by supposing a subject (mubtada'), or relating to its subject, or to both of them, since it contains their two pronouns; that is: "And indeed they bar them from the true path while they think that they are being guided to it." The use of the present tense (mudari') in the four verbs indicates continuous renewal, in accordance with His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 38:

﴿Until, when he comes to Us﴾ Although ḥattā (until) here is ibtidā'iyyah (introducing a new sentence) and is followed by a conditional clause, it necessarily implies that it is the endpoint (ghāyah) of a matter that extends over time, as has been mentioned many times before. The singular pronoun in "jā'a" (came) and what follows it is used because the intention is to relate the statement of each one of those who turn away (al-'āshūn) to his companion, in order to magnify the matter and make the state appear more dreadful. The meaning is: those who turn away continue in what was mentioned of pairing with the devils, and of the breast (al-ṣadr) and false supposition (al-ḥusbān al-bāṭil), until, when each one of them comes to Us together with his companion on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿He will say﴾ addressing him.

﴿"Would that between me and you were the distance of the two easts"﴾ in the world.

﴿"the distance of the two easts"﴾ i.e., the distance between the east and the west, that is, the remoteness of each of them from the other; so the east was given precedence and the dual form was used, and "distance" was attributed to both of them.

﴿"Wretched is the companion!"﴾ i.e., you.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 39:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And it will not benefit you﴾ ...etc. is a narration of what will be said to them at that time from Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as reproach and rebuke. That is: ﴿it will not benefit you﴾

﴿today﴾ means the Day of Resurrection, (p-48) your wishing, because of their distance [from you].

﴿since you wronged [yourselves]﴾ means: because of your wronging yourselves in the world by following them in disbelief and sins. It has also been said that ﴿since you wronged﴾ is a substitute for ﴿today﴾, meaning: since it has become clear to you and to all people that you wronged yourselves in the world. On this is the saying of the one who said: [When we trace our lineage, a base woman did not bear me], meaning: it has become clear that a base woman did not bear me, but rather a noble woman did.

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿that you will be sharing in the punishment﴾ is the reason for the negation of benefit, meaning: because it is fitting for you to share, you and your companions, in the punishment, just as you shared in its cause in the world. It is permissible that the verb be attributed to it, but not with the meaning that ﴿it will not benefit you﴾ is your sharing in the punishment, as the sharing of those who fall into the hardships of the world benefits them, since they cooperate in bearing its burdens and divide its toils, because each of them has a portion that his strength cannot bear, as it has been said. This is because benefiting in that way is not something that occurs to their minds, such that it would be refuted by negating it. Rather, the meaning is: you will not attain satisfaction by seeing your companions punished like you, since you used to pray against them by saying: "Our Lord, give them double punishment and curse them with a great curse" [Q 33:68], and your saying: "So give them a double punishment from the Fire" [Q 7:38], and similar expressions, so that you might find relief through that.

The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to strive hard in calling his people, while they increased only in misguidance and in feigning blindness to the signs of prophethood they witnessed, and in deafening themselves to the clear proofs of the Qur'an they heard. So [Allah] revealed:

Qur'anic quotation: ﴿Can you make the deaf hear, or guide the blind,﴾

This is a rhetorical question expressing wonder at the idea that he could be the one able to guide them, when they have grown accustomed to disbelief and immersed themselves in error, to the point that their blindness has become blindness combined with deafness.

﴿And whoever is in manifest error﴾ is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with "the blind," given the difference between the two descriptions. The point of the rhetorical denial lies in their being firmly established and settled in extreme error, such that there is no turning back from it, not in any supposed shortcoming on the part of the guide. Hence there is an allusion (ramz) to the fact that no one is able to accomplish this except God Most High alone, through compulsion and constraint.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 41:

﴿Whether We take you away﴾, i.e., if We take you (in death) before We show you their punishment, and thereby heal your breast and the breasts of the believers.

﴿Surely We will take vengeance upon them﴾ without doubt, in this world and in the Hereafter. Here "ma" is an emphasizing addition (ma muzidah li-l-ta'kid), standing in the same position as the oath particle lam (lam al-qasam) in that it never separates from the emphatic nun (al-nun al-mu'akkidah).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 42:

﴿Or We shall show you what We have promised them.﴾ That is: or We shall intend to show you the punishment that We have promised them.

﴿For indeed We have power over them﴾ in such a way that there is no escape for them from under Our dominion and Our subjugation. And indeed he (peace be upon him) was shown that on the Day of Badr.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 43:

﴿So hold firmly to that which has been revealed to you﴾ of the verses and the laws, whether We cause you to witness the promised (punishment) or We defer it until the Day of the Hereafter. It is also read as "awha" (أوحى) in the active voice, with the Agent being Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He.

﴿Indeed, you are upon a straight path﴾ is a reason (ta'lil) for the holding firmly, or for the command to do so.

﴿And indeed it is a reminder﴾ is a great honor.

﴿for you and your people. And you will be questioned﴾ on the Day of Resurrection about it, and about your upholding its rights.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 45:

﴿And ask those whom We sent before you of Our messengers.﴾ That is: ask their nations and the scholars of their religion, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So ask those who have been reading the Book before you.﴾ The benefit of this metaphor (majaz) is to alert that what is asked about is precisely what the tongues of the messengers uttered, not what their nations and scholars say from their own selves. Al-Farra' said: They only report it from the book of the messengers, so when he asks them, it is as if he asked the prophets, upon them be prayers and peace.

﴿Did We appoint gods besides the Most Merciful to be worshipped?﴾ That is: Did We ever decree the worship of idols, and did it come in any of their creeds (milal)? What is intended by this is the citation of the consensus of the prophets upon monotheism (tawhid), and an alert that it is not a novelty (bid'ah) that he invented, so that he should be denied and opposed.

﴿And We certainly sent Moses with Our signs﴾, being accompanied by them.

﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs, and he said, "Indeed I am a messenger of the Lord of the worlds."﴾ The purpose of relating his story is to console the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and to cite the call of Moses (peace be upon him) to tawhid (the affirmation of God's oneness), following the indication of the consensus of all the messengers (peace be upon them) on it.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 47:

﴿So when he brought them Our signs, behold, they laughed at them.﴾ That is: they were taken by surprise at the time of their laughing at them, i.e., they mocked them as soon as they saw them, and did not reflect upon them.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 48:

﴿And We did not show them any sign⁠﴾ — of the signs.

﴿except that it was greater than its fellow⁠﴾ — except that it was reaching the utmost degrees of inimitability (i'jaz), such that everyone who looks at it reckons it greater than all the signs compared with it. What is meant is describing all of them with the utmost greatness, without noticing any deficiency in any one of them; or [it means]: except that each one is distinguished by a kind of inimitability, being preferred over the others in that respect.

﴿And We seized them with the punishment⁠﴾ — such as the years of famine, the flood, the locusts, and others.

﴿so that they might return⁠﴾ — in order that they might turn back from the disbelief they were upon.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 49:

﴿And they said, "O sorcerer!"﴾ They addressed him thus in such a situation, owing to the extreme of their insolence and the utmost of their foolishness. It was also said: they used to call the learned, skilled man "sorcerer," because of their magnifying the knowledge of magic. It was read as "Ayyuhu al-sahiru" with a damma on the ha'.

﴿Pray to your Lord for us﴾ that He may remove the punishment from us.

﴿by what He has covenanted with you﴾ by His covenant with you concerning prophethood, or concerning the answering of your supplication, or concerning the removal of the punishment from those who are guided; or, "by what He has covenanted with you," meaning by what you fulfilled of faith and obedience.

﴿Indeed, we will surely be guided﴾ i.e., we will surely be believers, on the condition that the punishment is removed from us by your supplication, like their saying: ﴿If you remove from us the affliction, we will surely believe in you﴾.

﴿So when We removed the punishment from them﴾ at his supplication.

﴿Behold, they broke their word﴾ they were suddenly at the time of breaking their pledge to be guided. Its details have already been discussed in Surat al-A'raf.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 51:

﴿And Pharaoh proclaimed⁠﴾ in person, or through his herald.

﴿among his people﴾ in their assembly, and among themselves, after the punishment had been lifted from them, lest they believe.

﴿He said: "O my people, do not the kingdom of Egypt and these rivers belong to me﴾ — the rivers of the Nile, the greatest of which are four rivers: al-Malik (al-Malik), the river of Tulun, the river of Damietta, and the river of Tinnis.

﴿flowing beneath me﴾ — that is, beneath my palace or my command. It has also been said: beneath my throne, because of its height; and it has been said: before me, in my gardens and orchards. The waw here is either conjunctive, linking "these rivers" to "the kingdom of Egypt," so that "flowing" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of them; or it is a waw of the circumstantial clause, in which case "hādhihi" (this) is the subject (mubtada'), "al-anhār" (the rivers) is its attribute (ṣifa), and "tajrī" (flowing) is the predicate (khabar) of the subject.

﴿Do you not then see?﴾ — that, intending by it to magnify his kingdom.

﴿Or am I better﴾ than this one, with this kingdom and this ascendancy?

﴿than this one who is contemptible﴾, weak and insignificant, from al-muhanah (contemptibility), which means scarcity.

﴿and who can hardly make himself clear﴾. That is, the speech was said by them as a slander against him (peace be upon him) and as a belittling of him (peace be upon him) in people's eyes, in view of the speech impediment that was in his tongue (peace be upon him), a kind of ratta (lisp), which had been removed from him by the words of God Most High: ﴿You have been granted your request﴾. The "am" (أم) is either disjunctive (munqati'ah) and the hamzah is for affirmation, as if he said: after enumerating the causes of his excellence and the beginnings of his superiority, it is established and confirmed in your view that I am better, and this is my condition compared with this one ... etc. Or it is conjunctive (muttasilah), and the meaning is: "Do you not see? Or do you see?" except that he placed his saying "I am better" in the place of "you see," because when they said to him, "You are better," they were, in his view, perceptive people. This is of the type of placing the cause in the position of the effect. It is also permissible to take it as placing the effect in the position of the cause, since their sight, in respect of the causes of his excellence that were mentioned, is a cause in their opinion, for their judgement of his superiority.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 53:

﴿Why then have bracelets of gold not been cast upon him?﴾ That is: why were the keys of kingship (*maqalid al-mulk*) not delivered to him, if he were truthful? This is because they, when they made a man chief (*sawwadu*), would put a bracelet (*siwar*) on him and collar him with a gold necklace. *Aswira* is the plural of *siwar*. It has been read as *"asawir"*, the plural of *asware*, and as *"asawira"*, the plural of *iswar*, with the meaning of *siwar*, the ta replacing the ya of *asawir*. It has been read thus as well. It has also been read as *"alqa 'alayhi aswiratan"* and *"asawir"* in the active voice, with the subject being God the Exalted.

﴿or the angels come with him, accompanying him﴾ *Muqtarinin* means *maqrunin*, those who assist him or confirm him, from *qaranatuhu bihi* (I joined him to it), so *iqtarana* (he became joined). Or it means *mutaqarinin*, from *iqtarana*, with the meaning of *taqarana* (coming together).

**Then he made light of his people** — he provoked them and sought from them lightness (khiffah) in obeying him; or he made light of their minds (aḥlām).

**So they obeyed him** — in what he commanded them.

**Indeed they were a people who were defiant transgressors (fāsiqīn).** Therefore they hastened to obey that defiant transgressor, the misguided one (al-Ghawiyy).

**﴿فَلَمّا آسَفُونا﴾** — i.e., they angered Us to the utmost degree of anger. It is transferred (from its basic sense) from *asifa*, used when his anger became intense.

**﴿انْتَقَمْنا مِنهم فَأغْرَقْناهم أجْمَعِينَ﴾** — We took retribution from them and drowned them all, in the sea (*al-yamm*).

﴿So We made them a precedent﴾ (*salafan*), an example for those who came after them among the disbelievers, who would follow their path in deserving the like of the punishment that befell them. It is either a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) used as a qualifier, or the plural of *sālif*, as *khadam* is the plural of *khādim*. It was also read with a *ḍamma* on the *sīn* and the *lām*, as the plural of *salīf*, meaning a group that has passed on, like *rughuf*; or as *sālif*, like *ṣubur*; or as *salaf*, like *asad*. It was also read *"sulafan"* with the *ḍamma* of the *lām* changed to a *fatḥa*, or as the plural of *sulfah*, meaning a company that has passed on.

﴿and an example for the later ones﴾: that is, a lesson for them, or a wondrous story that travels as a proverb among them, so that it is said: "Your case is the case of the people of Pharaoh."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 57:

﴿When the son of Mary is cited as an example﴾ That is: Ibn al-Zib'ara struck this example when he disputed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) concerning His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, you and what you worship besides Allah are the fuel of Hell﴾, saying: "Is this for us and for our gods, or for all the nations?" The Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "It is for you and your gods and for all the nations." Then the accursed one said: "I have defeated you, by the Lord of the Ka'bah! Do not the Christians worship the Messiah, and the Jews worship 'Uzayr, and the Banu Mulayh worship the angels? If these are in the Fire, then we are content that we and our gods be with them." His people rejoiced at this and laughed, and their voices were raised. This is His words, exalted is He: ﴿when your people therefrom﴾, that is: from that example.

﴿yasiddun﴾ That is: a clamor and uproar rises up from them out of joy and exultation. It is also read as "yasuddun", meaning: because of that example they turn away from the truth, that is, they persist in the aversion they were already in, or increase in it. It was also said that it is likewise from ṣadīd (ṣadīd, meaning a loud outcry), and the two are dialectal variants of it, like yaʿkufu and yaʿkifu. The latter is more suitable to the meaning of suddenness (al-mufājaʾa).

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 58:

﴿And they say: "Are our gods better, or is he?"﴾ This is a quotation of part of the parable that they struck. They said it as a preface to what they built upon it of falsehood, dressed up with what deceives the foolish. That is: it is evident that Jesus is better than our gods, so since he is in the Fire, there is no harm in our being in the Fire with our gods. Know that what is reported of them, of joy and raised voices, was not because of what has been said, that he, peace be upon him, remained silent at that point until the words of God Most High were revealed: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has already preceded from Us﴾, and so on. That is because such a report, even with its implication of embarrassment (al-ifham, the implication that the Prophet was silenced) which must be cleared from his noble person, peace be upon him, from the very beginning, contradicts reality. How could it not? It has been reported that the statement of Ibn al-Zib'ara, "I have won against you, by the Lord of the Ka'bah," came from him at the very beginning, upon hearing the noble verse. The Prophet ﷺ replied to him, peace be upon him, saying: "How ignorant you are of the language of your people! Did you not understand that *ma* (what) is for that which does not reason?" He, peace be upon him, did not restrict this ruling to their gods when the disbeliever asked about the specific and the general, in accordance with what was mentioned about the word *ma* being specific to non-rational beings. This is because excluding some of the worshipped beings from it when needed would imply a concession to worshipping them in general. So he generalised it to all of them, but not by way of the explicit wording of the text (ibarat al-nass, the direct meaning of the words), rather by way of implication (dalalah, what follows from the text by inference), through the common factor of being worshipped besides God Most High. Then the Prophet, peace be upon him, made clear by his saying: "Rather, they worshipped the devils who commanded them to that," that the angels and the Messiah are far from being their worshipped ones, as is expressed by the words of God Most High: ﴿Glory be to You! You are our Protector, not them. Rather, they used to worship the jinn﴾, and so on. The reality of this matter has already been investigated at the words of God Most High: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best reward has already preceded from Us﴾, and so on. Rather, what they displayed of reprehensible conduct was only out of sheer impudence and their eagerness for stubbornness and obstinacy, as is expressed by the words of God Most High: ﴿They did not strike it for you except for argument﴾. That is: they did not strike that parable for you except for the sake of dispute and contention, not seeking the truth so that they would submit to it when it became manifest through your explanation.

﴿Rather, they are a people given to contention﴾. That is: they are fierce and vehement disputants, inclined to obstinacy and wrangling. It has also been said: when they heard the words of God Most High, ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus with God is like the likeness of Adam, whom He created from dust﴾, they said: "We are better guided than the Christians, because they worshipped a human, while we worship the angels." So the words of theirs, "Are our gods better, or is he?", at that point, were a preference of their gods over Jesus, peace be upon him, because what was meant by "they" was the angels. The meaning of "they did not strike it..." and so on is: they did not say this statement except for argument. It has also been said: when the verse ﴿Indeed, the likeness of Jesus﴾ was revealed, they said: "Muhammad does not intend by this except that we worship him, and that he deserves to be worshipped, even though he is a human, just as the Christians worshipped the Messiah, who was a human." The meaning of "yasiddun" is: they clamour and are vexed. The pronoun in "am" (or) refers to Muhammad, peace be upon him, and their purpose in weighing him against their gods was mockery of him. It has also been allowed that their intention was to disown what was denounced against them of their saying that the angels are the daughters of God Most High, and of their worship of them, as if they had said: "We have not uttered a novel statement, nor done a reprehensible deed, for the Christians made the Messiah the son of God and worshipped him, so we are more refined than them in word and deed, since we attributed to Him the angels, while they attributed to Him human beings."

Then His saying, ﴿It is but a servant upon whom We bestowed favor﴾, that is, with prophethood.

﴿And We made him an example for the Children of Israel﴾, that is, a wondrous matter, worthy that its mention should spread like the well-known proverbs. On the first reading, this is a resumptive clause (isti'naf), brought to declare the Messiah (peace be upon him) free from having attributed to him what was attributed to the idols by way of symbolism, as His saying, the Exalted, explicitly expresses: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best [reward] has preceded from Us﴾, and the verse. It also contains an alert to the invalidity of the opinion of those who raised him above the rank of servanthood, and an implicit criticism of the corruption of the opinion of those who hold their view concerning the angels. On the second and fourth readings, it serves to show that it is a false analogy based on a falsehood, or on something more false, according to their claim. And the Messiah is but a servant like all other servants. The utmost of his status is that he is among those whom We bestowed favor upon with prophethood, and We singled him out with some extraordinary distinctions, in that We created him in a wondrous manner, though We created Adam in a manner more wondrous than his. So where is he from the rank of lordship (rububiyya)? And from where could one imagine the validity of the doctrine of his worshippers, such that the worshippers of the angels would boast that they are better guided than them, or would plead that their condition is more exalted or more lowly than theirs? As for the third reading, it serves to refute them and to denounce them for their fabrication against the Messenger of God (ﷺ), by explaining that Jesus, in reality and in what was revealed to the Messenger, peace be upon them both, is nothing but a servant upon whom favor was bestowed, as has been mentioned. So how would he, peace be upon him, be pleased with being worshipped, or how could one imagine that he would be pleased with being worshipped as himself?

The phrase "﴿And if We willed﴾ ... etc." is given to establish that the case of Jesus, peace be upon him, is not a marvel beyond the power of God, and that He is able to do something more wondrous and more skillful than that. It also alerts the reader that the angels, too, have fallen from the rank of being worshipped. That is, Our power is such that ﴿if We willed﴾.

﴿We would have made⁠﴾, that is, We would have created by way of procreation.

﴿from among you⁠﴾, while you are men, and it is not in your nature to bear offspring.

﴿angels⁠﴾, as We created them by way of innovation (ibda').

﴿on the earth⁠﴾, settled in it, as We made them settled in the heaven.

﴿succeeding⁠﴾, that is, they would succeed you, like your children, in what you do and what you leave undone, and would undertake the acts that are assigned to your undertaking. Yet their nature is glorification and sanctification in the heaven. So if their nature is of this standing in relation to the Lordly power, how can it be imagined that they deserve worship, or that they are connected to Him, exalted be He far above that?

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 61:

﴿And indeed he﴾: and indeed 'Isa (Jesus, peace be upon him).

﴿is a sign (ʿilm) of the Hour﴾: meaning, by his descent he is one of its portents (ashrat al-sāʿah, the minor signs of the Hour), and calling him "ʿilm" is because the Hour is known through him, or because of his birth without a father, or because of his raising the dead. This is evidence for the truth of the resurrection (al-baʿth), which is the greatest of the matters concerning the Hour that the disbelievers deny. It is also read as "laʿalam," meaning "a sign" (ʿalāmah). It is read as "lil-ʿilm," and it is read as "la-dhikr," calling that which is mentioned by a thing "a remembrance," just as that by which knowledge is gained is called "knowledge." In a hadith: "'Isa, peace be upon him, will descend at a white minaret (thaniyyah) in the Holy Land called Afiq, wearing two saffron-dyed garments, with a spear in his hand, and with it he will kill the Dajjal (the false messiah). He will come to Bayt al-Maqdis while the people are at the dawn prayer, and the imam will hold back, so 'Isa, peace be upon him, will advance him, and pray behind him according to the law of Muhammad (ﷺ). Then he will kill the swine, break the cross, destroy the churches and synagogues, and kill the Christians, except those who believe in him." It was said: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, because it contains information about the Hour.

﴿So do not be in doubt about it﴾: so do not waver concerning its occurrence.

﴿And follow me﴾: meaning, follow my guidance, or my law (sharīʿah, the divine law), or my messenger. It was said: this is the words of the Messenger, commanded by the Most High.

﴿This﴾: meaning, that to which I call you, or the Qur'an, if the pronoun in "innahu" refers to it.

﴿is a straight path﴾: leading to the truth.

**Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 62:**

﴿And let not Satan avert you (from following Me).﴾

﴿Indeed, he is to you a manifest enemy.﴾ (He is) clear in enmity, in that he expelled your father from the Garden and exposed you to tribulation.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 63:

﴿And when Jesus came with clear proofs﴾ i.e., with the miracles, or with the verses of the Gospel (Injil), or with the manifest laws (shara'i').

﴿He said﴾ to the Children of Israel.

﴿Indeed, I have come to you with wisdom﴾ i.e., the Gospel, or the Law (shari'ah).

﴿And to make clear to you﴾ this is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon an implied clause indicated by the mention of coming with wisdom, as if it were said: "I have come to you with wisdom in order to teach it to you, and to make clear to you"

﴿some of that about which you differ﴾ namely, that which relates to matters of religion. As for what relates to matters of worldly affairs, clarifying it is not among the functions of the prophets, peace be upon them, as he, peace be upon him, said: "You are more knowledgeable about the affairs of your worldly life."

﴿So fear Allah﴾ by opposing me.

﴿And obey me﴾ in what I convey to you from Him, exalted is He.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 64:

﴿Indeed, Allah is my Lord and your Lord, so worship Him.﴾ This is an explanation of that which He commanded them to obey in it, namely the belief in Tawhid (the oneness of God) and the worship of God through the Sharia (divine law).

﴿This﴾ i.e., the Tawhid and the worship of God through the Sharia.

﴿is a straight path﴾ whose traveller does not go astray. It is either part of the speech of him, peace be upon him, or a fresh statement from the side of the Exalted, confirming the saying of Isa, peace be upon him.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 65:

﴿Then the factions differed﴾ the groups that formed parties (ahzab).

﴿from among them﴾ i.e., from among those to whom they were sent of the Jews and the Christians.

﴿So woe to those who did wrong﴾ from among those who differed.

﴿from the punishment of a painful day﴾ it is the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 66:

﴿Are they waiting for anything but the Hour, that it should come upon them⁠—﴾ That is: what are the people waiting for?

﴿Suddenly, while they are unaware⁠﴾ That is: "suddenly," but not while they are anticipating it; rather while they are heedless of it, occupied with the affairs of this world, denying it. This is His, the Exalted, saying: ﴿while they do not perceive﴾.

(p-54) ﴿Al-akhilla'﴾ (the close friends): those who love one another in the world, absolutely, or in worldly matters.

﴿Yawma'idhin﴾ (on that day): the day when the Hour comes upon them.

﴿Ba'duhum liba'din 'aduwwun﴾ (some of them will be enemies to others): because the bonds between them of close friendship and mutual love are severed, since it becomes evident that these were causes of punishment.

﴿Illa al-muttaqin﴾ (except the God-fearing): for their friendship in the world, since it was for the sake of God, remains as it was, and indeed increases, as each of them witnesses the effects of their friendship in reward and elevation of ranks. The exception is connected (muttasil) according to the first interpretation and disconnected (munqati') according to the second.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 68:

﴿O My servants, no fear shall be upon you this Day, nor shall you grieve﴾. This is a narration of what will be proclaimed to the God-fearing who love one another for the sake of God on that Day, as an honouring of them and a comforting of their hearts.

Verse 43:69: "Those who believed in Our signs and were Muslims."

"Those who believed in Our signs" is either an attributive qualifier of the addressed (al-munada) or is in the accusative of praise (nusiba 'ala al-mad-h).

"And they were Muslims" means: sincerely devoting their faces to Us, making their souls wholly submitted to Our obedience. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the waw of "amanu" (they believed). This is from Muqatil: when God raises the people, every one is struck with terror, and a caller calls out, "O My servants!" Then the creatures raise their heads in hope. Then "those who believed..." follows the verse, and the people of false religions lower their heads.

Enter the Garden, you and your spouses, joyfully. (Note: "your spouses" here are explained as "your wives who are believers.")

Translation of the commentary:

﴿Enter the Garden, you and your spouses﴾: your wives who are believers.

﴿You will be made joyful﴾: you will be made to rejoice with a joy whose trace (ḥabār) appears on your faces, i.e., its effect shows on your faces; or you will be adorned (tuzayyanūn) from ḥabra (ḥabra), which is fine appearance; or you will be honored with a great honor. And "al-ḥabra" (ḥabra): exaggeration in describing something with beauty.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 71:

﴿They will be served﴾ after their entry into Paradise, as they were commanded.

﴿with platters of gold and cups﴾ likewise. The "ṣiḥāf" (platters) is the plural of "ṣaḥfah," said to be like a "qaṣʿah" (large bowl). It is also said: the largest of the bowls is the "jafnah," then the "qaṣʿah," then the "makīlah." The "akwāb" (cups) is the plural of "kūb," which is a "kūz" (cup) without a handle.

﴿And therein﴾ i.e., in Paradise.

﴿is what the souls desire﴾ of the various kinds of delights. It has also been read as "mā tashtahī" (what the souls desire, with the verb in the feminine form).

﴿and that which the eyes delight in﴾ i.e., that which they find pleasure in and are gladdened by seeing. It has also been read as "wa-tulidhdhuhu" (and that which delights them, with the verb in the causative form).

﴿And you therein will abide forever﴾: this completes the blessing and perfects the joy, for every bliss has an end in this world, accompanied by fear of its loss, but in the Hereafter there is no such fear. The shift to direct address (iltifāt) is for honour.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 72:

﴿And that is the Paradise﴾ — a subject and predicate (mubtada' and khabar).

﴿which you have been made to inherit﴾ — and it is read "wurrithtumuhā" (with the verb in the intensive form, *warritha*, "you have been made to inherit").

﴿because of what you used to do﴾ — in the world, of righteous deeds. He likened the recompense of the deed to inheritance, because the doer is succeeded by it (yakhlufuhu al-'amil 'alayhi, "the worker inherits it from him"). It has been said: "That Paradise" is a subject (mubtada') and a qualifier (sifah), and the relative pronoun (al-mawsul) with its relative clause (silah) is its predicate (khabar). It has also been said: it is a qualifier of Paradise, as in the first view, and the predicate is ﴿because of what you used to do﴾, so the preposition (ba') is connected to an elided verb (mahdhuf), not to "you have been made to inherit," as in the first two views.

﴿For you therein is abundant fruit﴾ according to the kinds and varieties, (p-55) not merely according to the individual fruits.

﴿Of which you eat﴾, i.e., you eat some of it in every round, while the rest remains on the trees permanently. You will never see a tree in it that is empty of its fruit even for a moment; rather, they are always adorned with fruit and laden with it.

And it is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No man plucks from its fruit in Paradise except that another like it grows in its place."

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 74:

﴿Indeed, the criminals﴾ means: those firmly persisting in criminality (ijram), namely the disbelievers, as is indicated by their being mentioned in contrast to the believers in the verses.

﴿in the punishment of Hell will abide eternally﴾. The predicate of "inna" (indeed) is "fi 'adhab jahannam" (in the punishment of Hell), or "khalidun" (abiding eternally) is the predicate and "fi" (in) is related to it.

"They will not be lightened of it" — that is, the punishment will not be eased for them, from their saying: "The fever abated from him" (fatarat 'anhu al-humma) when it subsided a little; the root carries the sense of weakening.

"And they will be in it" — that is, in the punishment. It is also read "fīhā" (in it), meaning in the Fire.

"Despairing" — hopeless of deliverance.

**[Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 76]**

﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ by that.

﴿But it was they who were the wrongdoers﴾ because of their exposing themselves to the everlasting punishment.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 77:

﴿And they will call out﴾ to the keeper of the Fire.

﴿"O Malik!"﴾ It is also read "Ya Malu" (يا مالُ), by apocope (al-tarkhim, the clipping of the final letter of a vocative), with either damma or kasra. Perhaps this is an indication of their weakness and their inability to pronounce the word in full.

﴿"Let your Lord put an end to us!"﴾ That is: let Him cause us to die, so that we may find rest. From qada 'alayhi (قضى عليه), meaning: when He causes him to die. The meaning is: ask your Lord to put an end to us. This does not contradict what was mentioned of their despair, because it is a plea and a wish for death due to the extreme severity of the torment.

﴿He will say: "Indeed you will remain."﴾ That is: in the punishment forever, with no escape from it for you, neither by death nor by anything else. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he (the keeper) would not answer them until after a thousand years. It was said: after a hundred. It was said: after forty years.

Commentary of Abu al-Su'ud (Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim) on surah 43, verse 78:

﴿Indeed, We brought you the truth﴾ in the world, by sending the messengers and sending down the books. This is an address of reproach and rebuke from God, Exalted is He, which confirms the answer of Malik (the keeper of Hell) and explains the cause of their lingering. It has also been said that the subject of "qala" (he said) is God, Exalted is He.

﴿But most of you are averse to the truth﴾ — of whatever kind it was.

﴿averse﴾ — they do not accept it and recoil from it. As for the specific truth that is known, which is the Oneness of God or the Qur'an, then all of them are averse to it and repelled by it.

﴿Am abramū amran﴾ ("Or have they decided upon a matter?") is a new statement that censures the polytheists for the scheming they carried out against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). The "am" here is *munqati'ah* (disjunctive, introducing a new question), and what it carries of the meaning of "bal" (rather) serves to shift from rebuking the people of the Fire to recounting the offence of these people. The hamzah is for *inkar* (rejection). If by *ibram* (deciding firmly) one means actual firm determination, then the hamzah rejects that the event occurred and finds it unlikely. If one means firm determination in appearance only, then the hamzah rejects the reality and finds it abhorrent. That is, "Did the polytheists of Makkah decide upon a matter of their scheming and plotting against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?"

﴿Fa-inna mubrimūn﴾ ("then indeed We are the ones who decide") means: our scheme is real, not theirs; or, "then indeed We are the ones who firmly decide a scheme against them in reality, just as they firmly decided their scheme in appearance."
